The two gaṇas said: / 'O Śivaśarman of great intellect, this is the marvelous realm of Śukra. / Here dwells Kavi, the guru of the dānavas and daityas, / who, having inhaled the smoke of chaff, exceedingly unbearable, for a thousand years, / obtained from Hara the great vidyā that revives the dead. / Even the preceptor of the gods does not know this exceedingly difficult vidyā, / except for the Conqueror of Death, Skanda, Pārvatī, and the elephant-faced god.' / Śivaśarman said: / 'Who is this one known as Śukra, whose unexcelled realm this is? / And how was the vidyā that revives the dead obtained by him from Hara?
Tell this, O two lordly gods, if you have affection for me.'
Then those two gods related the supreme story of Śukra,
hearing which with faith, people are freed from untimely deaths,
and no fear arises from bhūtas, pretas, or piśācas.

Having spoken thus to the lord of the dānavas, Kavi recited the vidyā.
Designating each daitya one by one, they arose bearing their weapons,
like the Vedas constantly recited, or like rainclouds in the proper season,
or like wealth given with faith to brahmins in great calamity.
Seeing those great asuras, Tuhuṇḍa and the others, revived,
those elder gods roared like clouds filled with water.
Seeing those dānavas revived by Śukra, the lords of the gaṇas,
saying, 'This must indeed be reported to the Lord of Gods,' spoke thus to one another.
While that wondrous sacrifice of battle of the lords of pramathas was thus proceeding,
the son of Śilāda, indignant upon seeing the deed of Bhārgava, approached Maheśvara.
And saying 'Victory!', Nandī, radiant like gold, spoke to the fierce Source of Victory:
'O God, that exploit in battle of the gaṇa leaders, which is difficult even for the gods led by Indra,
has today been rendered futile for us by Bhārgava, by reviving those enemies dead in battle!'

If he continues to revive those struck-down foremost daityas again and again here,

Addressed thus by Nandin, lord of the pramathas, the Lord of the pramatha-lords,

and bring him here swiftly, just as a hawk carries off a quail chick!” 34
Addressed in this manner by the bull-bannered [Śiva], Nandin, whose roar was like a bull’s and a lion’s, roared;

Seeing his army being broken on all sides by the Pramathas,
Andhaka himself mounted his chariot and rushed against the Gaṇas.
Under those strikes of his thunderbolt-like arrows, as mountains struck by lightning-bolts,
the Pramathas could not hold their ground, like waterless clouds before the winds.
Observing each one retreating, advancing, far away, or near at hand,

wandering about searching for an opening, homeless like the wind,
beheld the seven worlds together with their guardians within Rudra's body.
He saw the manifold realms of Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, and Indra, and of the suns and the water-gods,
as well as the battle between the Pramathas and the Asuras.
Wandering all around within Bhava's belly for a hundred years,
he found no opening in him, just as a wicked man finds no flaw in an honest one.
Then, through the yoga of Śambhu, the descendant of Bhṛgu in the form of semen
fell forth and bowed low; then the god spoke to him:
“Since you came forth like semen (śukra), O son of Bhṛgu,
by this act you are Śukra, and you are my son; now depart.”
When Śukra emerged from his belly, the god too rejoiced greatly:
“It has turned out well for me while wandering, that the twice-born did not die in my belly.”
Having been spoken to thus by the god, Śukra, radiant like the sun,
entered the Dānava host like the moon entering a bank of clouds.
That great ocean of the Dānavas felt joy at Śukra's rising,
just as the great ocean garlanded with waves rejoices at the rising of the moon.

Having washed away entirely the great impurity of the mind called fickleness
with the waters of meditation repeatedly, together with the senses,
and making that jewel of the mind pure, offering it to the Wielder of Pināka,
the sage drank a stream of grain-husk smoke for a thousand autumns.
Then the god was pleased with the great-souled Bhārgava.
Emerging from that liṅga, surpassing the splendour of a thousand suns,
Virūpākṣa, the husband of Dākṣāyaṇī in bodily form, spoke:
“O treasury of austerity, I am pleased; choose a boon, O Bhārgava!”
Hearing this speech of Śambhu, the lotus-eyed twice-born,
his body bristling with horripilation from a surging abundance of bliss,
delighted, the corners of his eyes wide open, praised the eight-formed god,
placing his folded hands upon his head and crying, “Victory, victory!”
Bhārgava said:
“Overcoming all darkness with these rays of yours, you bring an end to the desires of the night-roamers; / you shine in the sky as a jewel for the welfare of the three worlds, O Lord of the Universe, therefore homage to you!
You shine as a jewel in the sky for the benefit of the three worlds, O Lord of the Universe, therefore homage to you!

You are the Wind on the pure path, ever-moving, worthy of worship; who here could live without you, the life of the world? / O motionless breaker, you make all creatures thrive, pleasing the serpents, omnipresent one, homage to you!
O wind that stills the gale, who nourish all creatures, who gladden the serpent race, who reach everywhere, therefore homage to you!
Except for the sole power of the Fire that purifies the whole universe and burns the sacrificer's offering, / can this world breathe, performing its immortal divine work like the gods? Ah, Inner Soul of the Universe, O Fire giving peace at every step, homage to you!
Ah, this universe breathes; O Inner Self of the universe, O Fire that grants peace at every step, homage to you!
O Supreme Lord in the form of water, purifier of the world, wondrous indeed is your variegated, noble conduct! / For this universe is made clean and pure, O Lord of the Universe, by drinking and bathing [in it]; therefore I bow down.

In the form of space, by giving room within and without, this universe blossoms here, O Īśvara; / from you, O compassionate one, it constantly breathes, and by its nature shrinks into you; therefore I bow to you.
From you always, O compassionate one, everything breathes by its nature and contracts; I am born of you, therefore I bow to you.

In the form of the earth, all-supporting, O Lord, who other than you could support this universe, O Lord of the Universe, enemy of darkness? / Therefore without you, O serpent-adorned husband of Himavat’s daughter, no other is to be praised by the tranquil; bowing to you who are beyond the highest, I bow.
Without you, O snake-adorned one, born of the snow-mountain, there is no other to be praised by the restrained; bowed to by the highest of the high, therefore I bow to you.
In the form of the Self, O Hara, this moving and unmoving form is pervaded by your successive forms; / dwelling as the inner self of all, mirroring every form, eternal one whose body is the Supreme Self, O eight-formed Lord, I constantly bow.
Dwelling as the inner self of all, possessing the form of every form, eternal, I bow to you whose body is the Supreme Self, O eight-formed Lord!
Thus by these eight forms, O you who are adored by Umā, most worthy of adoration, O Bhava whose form is beneficial to the universe! / This [universe] is pervaded and widely stretched out; O you who accomplish all aims, supreme reality for those who bow down, therefore I bow.
This is stretched out, widely extended, brought forth by those who bow; O ultimate reality, purpose of all desires, therefore I bow to you.
Having thus praised his chosen deity with this hymn of eight verses to the eight forms, Bhārgava,
his crown touching the ground of Śiva, bowed down again and again.
Thus praised by Bhārgava of exceedingly great splendour,
Mahādeva, raising the bowed twice-born from the earth with his arms and holding him,
spoke, illuminating the directions with the moonlight of his teeth:

4.16.m:
Whether women or men, whoever undertake a journey toward you—
by the cast of your glance, all their undertakings will come to ruin.
At your rising, O virtuous one, marriages and other rites—
all pious deeds among men here will be fruitful.
And all lunar days, even unpropitious ones, will be auspicious by conjunction with you.
Your devotees will have abundant semen and abundant offspring.
This liṅga installed by you, known as Śukreśa—
those men who worship it will attain siddhi.
Those men devoted to the nighttime fast on every Friday throughout the year,
and who perform all their water rituals at the Śukrakūpa well on your day,
and worship Śukreśa—hear the reward that awaits them!
Those mortals will have fruitful semen; they will have sons, with abundant virility;
they will be endowed with virile power and good fortune, of this there is no doubt.
Free from all obstacles, all those people shall live happily.'
Having granted these boons, the god dissolved into that liṅga.

Those who are devotees of Śukreśvara dwell in the realm of Śukra.
To the south of Viśveśvara stands Śukreśa, O scorcher of foes;
by merely seeing it, one is honored in the realm of Śukra.
Thus the condition of the realm of Śukra has been described, O wise one.
Agastya said:
While hearing this story of the realm of Śukra in this manner, O faithful wife of good vows,
that twice-born one then looked upon the realm of Aṅgāraka.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, entitled 'Description of the Realm of Śukra', in the first half of the Kāśīkhaṇḍa in the glorious Skandapurāṇa.
